l9ZqXlHl65g.summary: Veritasium's Derek Muller argues that Facebook's business model works against pages and creators, because it charges them to reach the audiences they built. He explains how filtering and paid promotion undermine the value of likes.
l9ZqXlHl65g.why: HN commenters recommend it, with its follow-up, as an exposé of fake likes and bot activity, and as a warning before spending on Facebook ads.

lJ8ydIuPFeU.summary: Gil Tene of Azul Systems explains common pitfalls in measuring latency and response time, including why averages mislead and the problem of coordinated omission. He introduces open source tools like HdrHistogram for better measurement and reporting.
lJ8ydIuPFeU.why: The canonical recommendation whenever percentiles, tail latency, load testing or averages come up, described by some as life changing.

lKXe3HUG2l4.summary: Joe Armstrong, co-inventor of Erlang, gives a funny and opinionated Strange Loop talk on the tangled state of software: build tools, package managers, entropy and the physical limits of computation. He argues for ideas like naming things by content hash and throwing away your first version.
lKXe3HUG2l4.why: HN returns to it constantly as a witty, still-accurate diagnosis of why software is bloated and messy, and as a go-to recommendation in any thread on modules, package managers or software quality.

l0GA901oGe4.summary: Seattle landscape architect Fred Young gives an hour-long visual tour of Dutch cycling infrastructure, covering design details, continuous networks and how cycling fits daily life in the Netherlands.
l0GA901oGe4.why: HN recommends it as an in-depth tech talk for urban planning, full of small design touches that make cycling safer.

l7TONauJGfc.summary: A roughly three-hour San Francisco workshop by Marshall Rosenberg on Nonviolent Communication, with full English subtitles added by a fan. He teaches the model with his jackal and giraffe language examples.
l7TONauJGfc.why: HN commenters send people to it as the primary source for NVC, recommended for relationships, compassion and difficult conversations.

l7rce6IQDWs.summary: Ben Eater explains how VGA signals work and builds a breadboard circuit that produces correct sync timing so a monitor recognizes the signal. He then builds toward displaying an image from simple logic chips.
l7rce6IQDWs.why: HN recommends it as a clear, from-scratch look at how video hardware works, understandable with just basic logic knowledge.

l8XOZJkozfI.summary: CGP Grey explains the Single Transferable Vote, a proportional ranked-ballot system, and why politicians have little incentive to adopt it. It is a short animated explainer of how multi-winner ranked voting works.
l8XOZJkozfI.why: HN's default link for explaining STV in any thread on voting reform, ranked choice or gerrymandering.

l_F9jxsfGCw.summary: Darius Kazemi's XOXO 2014 talk on releasing 72 weird internet side projects in a year. Framed as 'How I Won the Lottery,' it argues that success needs both luck and buying many tickets.
l_F9jxsfGCw.why: HN uses it as the favorite antidote to survivorship-bias success stories, arguing that trying many cheap things raises your odds.

lw6TaiXzHAE.summary: Guy Steele's classic 1998 OOPSLA keynote on how a programming language must grow with its user community. He delivers it in a playful style, starting with only monosyllabic words and defining new terms as he goes.
lw6TaiXzHAE.why: Treated as a must-watch for language designers, and cited whenever extensibility and language size are debated.

lkIicfzPBys.summary: Steve Yegge records himself working in Emacs and shows off about a dozen features in a roughly 45-minute screen capture. It is an informal, enthusiastic tour rather than a structured tutorial.
lkIicfzPBys.why: HN people recommend it as an excellent, convincing overview of Emacs for newcomers and skeptics, shown by someone who clearly loves it.

lHcTKWiZ8sI.summary: An Extra Credits episode on China's Sesame Credit, which gamifies obedient citizenship through a social score. It covers how the system rewards conformity and pressures people through their friends' behavior.
lHcTKWiZ8sI.why: HN commenters use it as a short, accessible primer on social credit and surveillance-driven gamification, linking it in many privacy and China threads.

lMcRBdSdO_U.summary: Aditya Siram introduces Shen, a small hosted Lisp with macros, a built-in Prolog and an optional type system. The talk demos a full web app moving between functional, logic and imperative styles, including turning JSON into a type with macros.
lMcRBdSdO_U.why: It is the standard recommended introduction to Shen, pointed to whenever Shen or its type system comes up.

l_aFHrzSBrM.summary: Adam Ragusea examines whether olive oil is unsafe for high-heat cooking and whether it tastes bad when heated. He cites studies showing it is among the most stable cooking oils and that smoke-point worries are overblown.
l_aFHrzSBrM.why: HN points to it to debunk the stubborn olive-oil-at-high-heat myth, valued for its cited sources and food scientist interviews.

lhYGXYeMq_E.summary: A long Machine Learning Street Talk interview with Kenneth Stanley, creator of NEAT and novelty search, about his book on why greatness cannot be planned. They discuss open-endedness, the tyranny of objectives, serendipity and the evolution of ideas.
lhYGXYeMq_E.why: Recommended to people who find it inspiring or perspective-changing on pursuing goals, open-ended search and AI beyond optimization.

l70iRcSxqzo.summary: Kim Nilsson presents his investigation into how Mt. Gox was hacked and mismanaged, tracing the finances and the missing bitcoins. It was given at the 2017 Breaking Bitcoin meetup.
l70iRcSxqzo.why: HN commenters call it one of the best, most unbiased explanations of what actually happened to Mt. Gox and its missing coins.

lnnsDi7Sxq0.summary: A 2018 GDC panel where Raph Koster, Starr Long, Richard Garriott and Rich Vogel look back on what went right and wrong building and running Ultima Online. They share candid stories from the early days, including player behavior and server architecture.
lnnsDi7Sxq0.why: HN recommends it as a transparent MMO postmortem and as the source of the story that the term 'shard' originated with Ultima Online.

lG4VkPoG3ko.summary: 3Blue1Brown explains why positive results on accurate medical tests are often false positives, and reframes Bayes' rule using likelihood ratios (Bayes factors) to update odds. It uses visual examples to make the reasoning intuitive.
lG4VkPoG3ko.why: HN's go-to link whenever Bayesian reasoning, base rates or imperfect tests come up.

lJ3NC-R3gSI.summary: Steve Klabnik walks through the history of Rust and how its design evolved toward async/await, including the alternatives tried and dropped. He also discusses the difficulty of adding a major feature to a language.
lJ3NC-R3gSI.why: HN points to it to show how deliberately the Rust team arrived at async/await and why it was chosen over alternatives like green threads.

lkgszkPnV8g.summary: Louis Brandy presents the most common and infamous recurring C++ bugs seen in Facebook's huge codebase, including shared_ptr data races and operator[] pitfalls. He explains the surprising complexity behind seemingly simple code.
lkgszkPnV8g.why: HN recommends it as a must-watch catalogue of C++ footguns, often cited in debates about Rust and C++ safety.

l6T9xIeZTds.summary: Tesla's 2020 Battery Day event, with a company update and a keynote on new cell design, manufacturing, vertical integration and cheaper lithium and materials. It ends with the Plaid Model S and a Q&A.
l6T9xIeZTds.why: Treated as the essential primary source for Tesla's battery and cost-reduction plans, and a feast for engineering nerds.

l6XQUciI-Sc.summary: A BSD Now episode featuring a long interview with Joyent CTO Bryan Cantrill on dtrace, ZFS, pkgsrc, containers and more. It includes his rant on why Linux epoll is flawed and stories from Sun.
l6XQUciI-Sc.why: HN links it for Cantrill's entertaining epoll versus kqueue rant and his stories, such as bricking a machine with rm -rf.

lG2dXobAXLI.summary: A videogamedunkey video essay on video game critics. It argues that a critic's taste and integrity matter as much as their score, and tries to explain why major outlets give such inflated ratings.
lG2dXobAXLI.why: Recommended as an amusing but thoughtful take on review inflation and game journalism, in threads about reviews and ratings.

lPgZfhnCAdI.summary: A Daily Show with Jon Stewart segment from 2014 covering the People's Climate March in New York and a House science committee struggling with basic global warming facts. It mixes satire with an argument against climate denial.
lPgZfhnCAdI.why: Commenters call it a favorite Daily Show clip and link it as a ready answer to climate-skeptic arguments.

lY8Ol2n4o4A.summary: Ian Hubert shows how to use Blender's motion tracking to turn ordinary footage of a room into a stylized digital environment for an indie film. It is a quick, practical walkthrough in his loose, lazy-tutorial style.
lY8Ol2n4o4A.why: Recommended as an eye-opening, fast introduction to what Blender can do and a model of a productive workflow.

la-sGpTpkxE.summary: Mike of mikeselectricstuff shows his heavily modified old BBC Micro system in a 28-minute tour of 8-bit hardware archaeology.
la-sGpTpkxE.why: Recommended as an entry point to a favorite electronics channel, valued for deep knowledge and no showy bravado.

ljOoGyCso8s.summary: Strange Parts tours JLCPCB's large PCB factory in Huizhou, China, walking through the printed circuit board manufacturing process step by step. It shows the machinery, quality checks and scale behind cheap prototype boards.
ljOoGyCso8s.why: Recommended as the best look inside a modern PCB fab, cited in threads on hobby PCB vendors, manufacturing in China and automation.

lyqt6u5_sHA.summary: A CAD-based animation from the Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics showing how the Wendelstein 7-X stellarator is configured and what its fusion research aims to achieve. It runs about 11 minutes.
lyqt6u5_sHA.why: HN links it in stellarator and fusion threads as an understandable look at the design and engineering challenges.

l4dCJJFuMsE.summary: A three-minute clip of Steve Jobs arguing that great products come from people who care about content rather than process. He says process-focused people take over and cause decline, citing IBM as an example.
l4dCJJFuMsE.why: Quoted whenever HN discusses process-heavy management and companies losing their product focus.

lHLpKzUxjGk.summary: John Carmack speaks at UMKC's 2017 commencement event about the difficulties of VR, especially end-to-end latency across hardware and software. He covers why latency and buffering matter and how nausea is addressed.
lHLpKzUxjGk.why: Recommended whenever latency, buffering or VR comfort comes up, as an accessible account from someone who dealt with it directly.

lIW5jBrrsS0.summary: A short film by Max Joseph about his anxiety in bookstores and how to read more books amid constant streaming, social media and news. He looks for ways to rebalance his content diet in favor of reading.
lIW5jBrrsS0.why: HN commenters cite it as a thoughtful mini-doc on reading time and frequency in the age of social media.

lcjdwSY2AzM.summary: Veritasium explores why energy is not conserved in general relativity, using Emmy Noether's theorem linking symmetries to conservation laws. Physicists interviewed explain energy loss in an expanding universe.
lcjdwSY2AzM.why: Recommended as high-quality physics communication and as an introduction to Noether and energy non-conservation in cosmology.

lsDc1YVxHA0.summary: In the finale of Double Fine's Devs Play, speedrunner SMK demonstrates glitches and exploits that skip entire sections of Psychonauts while Tim Schafer and the dev team watch. The developers react to and discuss the bugs as they appear.
lsDc1YVxHA0.why: Recommended as an entertaining, hilarious view of developers watching a speedrunner break their game.

lI7T650RTT8.summary: Armor expert The Chieftain explains why tanks still have a place on the modern battlefield despite drones and guided weapons. He responds to the 'tank is dead' debate, noting that tanks have been declared dead repeatedly since 1919.
lI7T650RTT8.why: Pointed to as an authoritative answer, from a former Abrams commander and tank historian, to claims that tanks are obsolete.

lIFE7h3m40U.summary: Tom Scott explains how he built his emoji keyboard, which turned out to be a series of bodged-together tools including AutoHotkey and LuaMacros. He tells stories about the value of quick-and-dirty solutions.
lIFE7h3m40U.why: HN links it as a charming defense of bodging and of AutoHotkey, and as the go-to example when custom keyboards or hotkey hacks come up.

lKQ0yaEJjok.summary: Joscha Bach's 31c3 talk argues that the mind should be understood as an information-processing system and that even the physical universe can be seen as computational. It tours the philosophy underlying artificial intelligence and cognitive science.
lKQ0yaEJjok.why: HN recommends it as an inspiring summary of a computational model of mind and a first lecture in a series on the brain as a computer.

lWZ2Bz0tS-s.summary: The first lecture of an MIT course on Douglas Hofstadter's Godel, Escher, Bach, covering themes like self-reference, recursion and incompleteness. The full lecture series is on YouTube.
lWZ2Bz0tS-s.why: Recommended as a companion to reading the dense book.

lXfEK8G8CUI.summary: A Kurzgesagt animation giving a big-picture tour of the human immune system, its organs, transport network, and the cells it produces every day. It accompanies their IMMUNE book.
lXfEK8G8CUI.why: HN commenters suggest it as a simple, well-made introduction to how immune responses work when discussing infection, T cells or chronic illness.

leX541Dr2rU.summary: Tom Scott's Royal Institution discourse on science communication in the age of social media, how recommendation algorithms shape popularity, and why view counts can matter more than truth. It includes a segment on parasocial relationships.
leX541Dr2rU.why: HN returns to it in discussions of algorithmic feeds, misinformation and parasocial relationships, as a clear and thoughtful talk.

lgivCGdmFrw.summary: John McCall of Apple's Swift team presents at CppNow 2023 on introducing a memory-safe successor language into large C++ code bases. He argues incremental improvement of C++ hits hard limits and explains Swift's C++ interoperability for gradual migration.
lgivCGdmFrw.why: Used as the primary source for Apple's stated plan to make Swift its successor to C++ and for how interop supports gradual transition.

lhe286ky-9A.summary: A short RepresentUs explainer on how money corrupts American politics and what an anti-corruption act could do about it. It covers lobbying, super PACs and campaign finance, and pitches the group's proposed reforms. The video was later superseded by an updated version.
lhe286ky-9A.why: HN commenters cite it as a brief summary of the problem and the proposed Anti-Corruption Act solution when arguing for getting money out of politics.

lnA9DMvHtfI.summary: A short cartoon explaining how language models like ChatGPT work, from autocomplete and conditional probabilities to neural networks, gradient descent and backpropagation. It shows how networks act as universal function approximators.
lnA9DMvHtfI.why: HN recommends it as a quick, non-dumbed-down way to get up to speed on how LLMs are built.

loCBvaj4eSg.summary: Andres Gomez Emilsson of the Qualia Research Institute presents a model of DMT experiences using hyperbolic geometry and dynamical systems theory. He describes how different intoxication levels correspond to changing curvature and information content of experience.
loCBvaj4eSg.why: HN commenters point to it as an interesting lecture related to psychedelics, brain geometry and hyperbolic space, with a good intro to hyperbolic geometry.

lqzJewjZUkk.summary: Fraser Cain interviews JPL physicist Slava Turyshev about using the Sun's gravity as a lens to image distant exoplanets. They cover how the lens works, how a spacecraft would align with it, and mission design.
lqzJewjZUkk.why: HN points to it as the best accessible explanation of the solar gravitational lens mission plan.

lr4MmmWQtZM.summary: Joseph Everett compares the food environment of the US, with roughly 30% obesity, to Japan's, around 3.5%. He argues that what is available and normal to eat explains much of the gap.
lr4MmmWQtZM.why: HN commenters recommend it as an accurate account of everyday Japanese eating and of why the US food environment is so much worse.

lvTqbM5Dq4Q.summary: MinutePhysics explains Shor's algorithm, showing how a quantum computer factors large integers by finding the period of a number modulo N. It walks through the modular arithmetic and number theory that give the exponential speedup over classical factoring, and why this threatens encryption.
lvTqbM5Dq4Q.why: HN commenters point to it as a clear, approachable explanation of Shor's algorithm and what quantum computers actually do.

l9ag2x3CS9M.summary: Military History Visualized charts ship production by the United States and Japan from December 1941 to September 1945. The growing numbers show why Japan, despite a stronger starting navy, could not win a long war.
l9ag2x3CS9M.why: Cited as one of the best visualizations of how overwhelmingly dominant US industrial output was in the Pacific war.

lC4YLMLar5I.summary: An hour-long video essay on Elite, the 1984 BBC Micro game by David Braben and Ian Bell. It covers how they fit a 3D engine, economy and universe into 22KB on a 2MHz 6502.
lC4YLMLar5I.why: HN commenters recommend it as an amazing overview of the technical feats and history behind Elite, and cite it for what the 6502 could do.

lFXJWPhDsSY.summary: agadmator walks through a game in which DeepMind's AlphaZero beat Stockfish, ending in a famous zugzwang that leaves the engine helpless. He gives commentary on the moves.
lFXJWPhDsSY.why: HN recommends it as a striking, well-explained example of AlphaZero's play and of zugzwang.

lX-K63pVPTM.summary: An excerpt from an RSA event in which physicist David Deutsch makes the case for optimism as a driver of progress in the 21st century. It is a short highlight of a longer discussion.
lX-K63pVPTM.why: Pointed to as an antidote to pessimism about the future, tied to Deutsch's ideas in The Beginning of Infinity.

lqJUIqZNzP8.summary: Robert Miles introduces the first of several videos on the paper 'Concrete Problems in AI Safety', focusing on how AI systems can cause accidental negative side effects. It explains the problem in accessible terms.
lqJUIqZNzP8.why: HN recommends Robert Miles' channel as a clear starting point for people curious about AI safety.

l3whaviTqqg.summary: Rational Animations explains Robin Hanson's grabby aliens model, which argues that humanity looks suspiciously early in cosmic history. Expanding civilizations set a deadline that explains our timing and bears on the Fermi paradox.
l3whaviTqqg.why: Recommended as a short explanation of a non-intuitive anthropic reasoning argument.

lBVvnDfW2Xo.summary: Technology Connections explains what forced-air furnaces are, how they work and why they need electricity. He covers combustion, airflow and the parts of a modern furnace.
lBVvnDfW2Xo.why: HN people point to it as the full explanation of how gas furnaces work, mostly in threads on heating, power outages and gas appliances.

lD9FAOPBiDk.summary: A two-minute Microsoft ad for Internet Explorer 10 in which a karaoke-style song addresses people who hate the browser. It is part of the "browser you loved to hate" campaign.
lD9FAOPBiDk.why: Cited in threads about IE's reputation as an example of Microsoft's self-aware, funny advertising.

lDfjdGva3NE.summary: Isaac Yonemoto's ElixirConf 2021 talk on Zigler, a library for writing Elixir NIFs in Zig. He looks at its internals and how it bridges the two languages while keeping the NIFs well behaved on the BEAM.
lDfjdGva3NE.why: HN threads on Zig and Elixir link it as the creator's explanation of how Zig NIFs can behave nicely inside the BEAM.

le71yVPh4uk.summary: Jim Browning reverses a scammer's remote connection and discovers CCTV in a Delhi call centre. He gives a detailed look at how a tech support scam operation runs, and he shared the footage with the BBC.
le71yVPh4uk.why: HN points to it as a fascinating inside look at how Indian scam call centres operate, often when scams come up in discussion.

leFuF-zoVzA.summary: Strange Parts builds a working refurbished iPhone 6S entirely from components bought in the Huaqiangbei phone parts markets in Shenzhen. The video explains how the markets work and what the parts cost.
leFuF-zoVzA.why: HN cites it as proof that a full iPhone can be assembled from sourced parts, in right-to-repair and Shenzhen hardware ecosystem discussions.

lfo8XHGFAIQ.summary: Real Engineering examines whether greening the Sahara could draw down carbon and slow climate change. It concludes that the effort would be enormously costly and that changes in albedo and other effects undercut the climate benefit.
lfo8XHGFAIQ.why: Recommended in tree-planting and carbon removal threads as a sourced explanation of why greening deserts is not a simple climate fix.

lix-vr_AF38.summary: LightningOnDemand revives a pulsed Lorentz plasma cannon, using modern capacitors to extend its range and increase the delivered energy. It is a high-voltage, high-current hobby demonstration.
lix-vr_AF38.why: HN users suggest it to anyone who enjoys extreme high-voltage projects and big capacitor-bank discharges.

lpu-3UF_b48.summary: Curtis Poe's FOSDEM talk arguing that day-to-day Perl 6 is far simpler than its enthusiasts' talk of exotic features suggests. He compares basic math and string handling across languages.
lpu-3UF_b48.why: Offered as a pragmatic, convincing counter to the idea that Perl 6 is too strange to use.

lwhMThePdIo.summary: A Microsoft Build 2019 session in which the WSL team explains the new WSL 2 architecture, which runs a real Linux kernel alongside Windows on a hypervisor. It covers faster file performance, Linux file access from Windows and better application support.
lwhMThePdIo.why: HN points to it as the authoritative source for how WSL2 works and why Microsoft rebuilt it.

lyu7v7nWzfo.summary: Neuroscientist Anil Seth argues in this TED talk that perception is a controlled hallucination: the brain constantly predicts the world and our shared agreement is what we call reality. He also touches on the construction of the self.
lyu7v7nWzfo.why: HN cites it whenever threads touch consciousness, perception or predictive-processing, especially for its examples of expectation changing what you perceive.

lzsZP9o7SlI.summary: John Oliver's Last Week Tonight segment on homeschooling, focusing on how little regulation exists in many US states. It covers states where a one-time declaration removes children from any oversight.
lzsZP9o7SlI.why: HN commenters use it as a researched, eye-opening reference whenever homeschooling oversight comes up.

l4w6808wJcU.summary: CGP Grey discusses flag design principles and grades flags, following the Minnesota state flag redesign. It argues for simple, distinctive flags.
l4w6808wJcU.why: Linked whenever flag redesigns come up, and credited as hugely influential on how people think about flag design.

l0P4Cf0UCwU.summary: UnHerd interviews Wikipedia co-founder Larry Sanger, who explains why he no longer trusts the site he helped create. He argues that it has become biased and is no longer a neutral, open platform.
l0P4Cf0UCwU.why: HN commenters cite it as an authoritative-sounding critique of Wikipedia's bias, coming from one of its own founders.

l4UgZBs7ZGo.summary: Technology Connections explains how analog television produced moving images without computers, covering scanning, CRTs and standards like NTSC and PAL. It is part of a series on analog TV.
l4UgZBs7ZGo.why: HN points to it as a clear explainer of how analog TV and CRTs actually work, and as the entry point to the author's wider TV series.

lBfVxBj61z0.summary: Jellyvision hosts Basecamp founders Jason Fried and David Heinemeier Hansson for a Q&A about open source, productivity, feature requests and taking care of customers.
lBfVxBj61z0.why: HN points to it as an example of the founders' realistic, down-to-earth approach and their bootstrapped, lifestyle-business philosophy.

lGEMwh32soc.summary: A React Conf talk by Xuan Huang previewing React Forget, a compiler that automatically memoizes components. It argues for making memoization the default so developers need not write useMemo or useCallback by hand.
lGEMwh32soc.why: Shared in discussions of useCallback and memoization as the first look at where React was heading with an auto-memoizing compiler.

lKhAd0Tyny0.summary: Primatologist Frans de Waal shows an experiment in which capuchin monkeys refuse a reward after seeing a partner get a better one for the same task. It illustrates a sense of fairness in primates.
lKhAd0Tyny0.why: HN cites it in discussions of pay fairness and inequality as a short, funny demonstration of the fairness instinct.

lLcpcytUnWU.summary: A three-minute clip of Noam Chomsky in an exchange with BBC journalist Andrew Marr about media filtering and self-censorship. Chomsky argues that people reach positions precisely because they would not say things that conflict with the system.
lLcpcytUnWU.why: Cited as the source of Chomsky's 'you wouldn't be sitting where you're sitting' line in threads on media bias and corporate employees defending their employers.

lR0nh-TdpVg.summary: Christopher Domas's Black Hat 2015 talk on a long-unnoticed x86 design flaw that lets an attacker reach System Management Mode, a ring below the OS. It explains how the legacy architecture allows universal privilege escalation and persistent, hard-to-detect malware.
lR0nh-TdpVg.why: Cited in discussions of CPU hidden features, Intel's security failures and SMM malware as a concrete example of a forgotten processor feature being exploited.

lRndE7rSXiI.summary: Gernot Heiser presents seL4, a microkernel with a mathematical proof connecting security properties to the binary code, and explains what its open-sourcing means for users. It covers its roles as a microkernel, separation kernel and hypervisor.
lRndE7rSXiI.why: Cited to explain what formal verification of seL4 guarantees, such as ruling out whole classes of bugs like buffer overflows.

leNaS9eJWqo.summary: A three-minute capture of SORTDEMO.BAS, the sorting visualization that shipped with QBasic. It animates insertion, bubble, heap, exchange, shell and quick sort with chiptune-like sound.
leNaS9eJWqo.why: HN fondly recalls it as the ideal visual demonstration of sorting algorithms and as the thing that got some people into programming.

ljPFZrRD3J8.summary: The Rubberbandits perform "Horse Outside", a comic Irish song about a horse waiting outside, from the RTE show Republic of Telly.
ljPFZrRD3J8.why: Shared as a delightful example of Irish humor and as a joke reference.

lnq-2BJwatE.summary: Neal Stephenson visits Google in 2008 to discuss his novel Anathem as part of the Authors@Google series. He talks about the book's world and takes audience questions.
lnq-2BJwatE.why: HN uses it mainly as the place where Stephenson addresses criticism of his novels' endings, plus as a fun author talk with jokes.

lsWndfzuOc4.summary: A roughly 2.5-hour Toronto debate between Jordan Peterson and Slavoj Zizek on happiness under Marxism versus capitalism. This is the official upload from April 2019.
lsWndfzuOc4.why: HN uses it as a reference for Zizek's views and as an exercise in critical thinking, not as a strong recommendation.

l2ThMmgQdpE.summary: A short 2000s Apple commercial for the PowerMac G4 that plays on the computer being classed as a weapon under US export restrictions, with tanks as imagery.
l2ThMmgQdpE.why: Cited as a clever precedent whenever export controls on powerful computing hardware or AI models are discussed.

lAtVOK04XvA.summary: A short Inside Edition segment on Daniel Kish, a blind man who uses tongue clicks as human sonar to ride a bicycle through city traffic. He explains that he hears the reflections of the sounds off objects.
lAtVOK04XvA.why: Cited as a concrete example that humans can learn echolocation, in threads about animal and human sonar.

lC5lsemxaJo.summary: A short clip from The Office US in which Michael Scott gets drawn into an email scam promising riches from the son of a deposed Nigerian king. It plays on pyramid schemes and gullibility.
lC5lsemxaJo.why: Used as a joke reference whenever crypto, Worldcoin or AI hype seems like a scheme out of a sitcom.

lEplzHraw3c.summary: Cloth Map documents Havana's SNET, a community-built private network that Cubans created because internet prices were high. It is used for gaming and sharing.
lEplzHraw3c.why: Cited as context for Cuba's Street Net and as an example of grassroots networks built under constraints.

lFIYKmos3-s.summary: A short excerpt from a 1973 Yorkshire TV film in which Richard Feynman explains that knowing the name of something is not the same as knowing it.
lFIYKmos3-s.why: Shared to end arguments over definitions and terminology, and as a reminder that memorizing names is not understanding.

lKie-vgUGdI.summary: A short clip from the TV sitcom Arrested Development in which Tobias delivers the line 'There are dozens of us... DOZENS'. It is an uploaded excerpt of the show, not original content.
lKie-vgUGdI.why: Commenters quote it as a punchline when a group claims to be larger or more significant than it is.

lMChO0qNbkY.summary: A satirical Onion news segment announcing a Google feature that lets users opt out of Google's data collection by moving to a remote village without Google products or sunlight.
lMChO0qNbkY.why: Used as a punchline in privacy and opt-out threads, mostly as a joke that reality has caught up to the satire.

lNX0wCdD2LA.summary: A one-minute NVIDIA research demo of foveated rendering for VR using SMI eye tracking. It renders at full detail only where the eye is looking, matching the physiology of human vision.
lNX0wCdD2LA.why: Used as a visual example of how foveated rendering can cut the GPU power needed for VR.

lNYcviXK4rg.summary: The official video for 'Da Da Da' by the German Neue Deutsche Welle band Trio, a sparse, minimalist pop song. The track uses a cheap Casio VL-1 keyboard as its core sound.
lNYcviXK4rg.why: Cited as an example of minimalist pop production and as the song that made the Casio VL-1 famous.

lNdb03Hw18M.summary: A three-minute side-by-side comparison of scenes from Star Wars (1977) and the WWII film The Dam Busters (1955). It shows how closely the Death Star trench run mirrors the earlier film.
lNdb03Hw18M.why: HN links it whenever the topic of Star Wars borrowing from WWII films comes up, as direct visual evidence.

lOTyUfOHgas.summary: A short clip from The Simpsons episode "Hurricane Neddy" containing the line "We've tried nothing and we're all out of ideas."
lOTyUfOHgas.why: Invoked as a joke reference when someone seems to give up or ask for help without trying anything.

lUQ_0MubbcM.summary: A short clip of Noam Chomsky explaining why the United States supports Israel, framing it in terms of strategic interests and foreign policy. It is posted by a channel that collects his talks.
lUQ_0MubbcM.why: Used as a source for the argument that US support for Israel is systematic and strategic, and for Chomsky's view of Palestine as resistance to colonialism.

lXUZvyajciY.summary: Dwarkesh Patel interviews Andrej Karpathy on why reinforcement learning is flawed, why AGI may blend into steady GDP growth, why self-driving took so long, and the future of education. The conversation runs about two and a half hours.
lXUZvyajciY.why: Mostly cited as a source for Karpathy's views on agents, AGI timelines and LLMs, rather than recommended outright.

lay8aZlsbB0.summary: A one-minute clip filmed from the Arc de Triomphe showing chaotic multi-lane traffic in the surrounding roundabout, including a bus trying to cross about six lanes.
lay8aZlsbB0.why: Used as a vivid example of chaotic roundabout traffic when discussing road design and driving in Europe.

lc5Np9OqDHU.summary: A short video built around Douglas Crockford, creator of JSON, saying JavaScript is a flawed language and that developers should eventually move on from it. It is a brief commentary clip with little technical detail.
lc5Np9OqDHU.why: HN users cite it to show that even Crockford, once a JavaScript evangelist, has soured on the language, though some find it thin on substance.

lc7scxvKQOo.summary: A short clip demonstrating a phone-based social engineering trick in which a crying baby in the background is used to pressure a customer service rep. It shows how attackers exploit human sympathy rather than technical flaws.
lc7scxvKQOo.why: Cited as a funny and effective real example of social engineering whenever support-desk account takeovers and human weak points are discussed.

lj3iNxZ8Dww.summary: A one-minute clip of Miss Teen USA 2007 contestant Miss South Carolina giving a rambling, incoherent answer to a pageant question. It became a widely shared internet meme.
lj3iNxZ8Dww.why: Only posted as a joke reaction to someone's muddled or incoherent argument, not as something to watch for content.

ljx0Zh7eidE.summary: Computer History Museum oral history of Steve Naroff, an engineer at Stepstone, NeXT and Apple who worked on Objective-C. This first session covers his childhood, music background and early career.
ljx0Zh7eidE.why: Pointed to as a primary-source account of Objective-C's origins and the early days of NeXT and Apple.

lkjyeI0ykGM.summary: EEVblog's Dave Jones critiques Reflect Orbital's plan to sell sunlight to solar farms after dark using orbital mirrors. He walks through the numbers to show the idea does not work out.
lkjyeI0ykGM.why: HN cites it as a debunking whenever the space mirror startup comes up, as a TL;DW that the design is impractical.

ll3CMgiUPuU.summary: The full 1965 John Coltrane album A Love Supreme, in four parts: Acknowledgement, Resolution, Pursuance and Psalm. It features Coltrane's quartet with McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison and Elvin Jones.
ll3CMgiUPuU.why: Mentioned as an example of spiritual, non-romantic love in music and as a demanding jazz work that is hard for the uninitiated.

llRkf1fnNDM.summary: A two-minute minutephysics video explaining why turning a bicycle requires first steering briefly the other way. It covers counter-steering and balance with slow-motion footage and 3D animation.
llRkf1fnNDM.why: HN cites it as a quick illustration of countersteering, the idea that you must first turn the opposite way to lean into a turn.

lncLOEqc9Rw.summary: A George Carlin stand-up bit proposing a war on homelessness, mocking how every national problem is framed as a war. It is a satirical routine about homelessness and housing.
lncLOEqc9Rw.why: Quoted as a comedic aside in threads on homelessness and housing, where commenters note it lands on the same conclusion as serious articles.

lskpNmUl8yQ.summary: A short clip of Bill Gates appearing on David Letterman's show in 1995 trying to explain the value of the internet. Letterman is visibly unconvinced.
lskpNmUl8yQ.why: HN cites it as an example of how even sharp people dismissed a transformative technology, often invoked in crypto debates.

lugeruSbnAE.summary: A short South Park clip from the 'Post COVID: The Return of COVID' special in which Stan relies on his Alexa. It plays on voice assistants responding to their wake word.
lugeruSbnAE.why: HN mostly uses it as a joke or a demonstration of Alexa waking up on cue.
